This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal and $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$. Let $r\geq 1$. Must $G$ contain a subgraph of chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ which does not contain any odd cycle of length $\leq r$?
#740: [Er69b][Er71,p.100][Er81][Er95d]
graph theory | 
chromatic number
A question of Erdős and Hajnal. Rödl proved this is true if $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_0$ and $r=3$ (see [108] for the finitary version).
More generally, Erdős and Hajnal asked must there exist (for every cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$ and integer $r$) some $f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ such that every graph with chromatic number $\geq f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ contains a subgraph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ with no odd cycle of length $\leq r$?
Erdős [Er95d] claimed that even the $r=3$ case of this is open: must every graph with sufficiently large chromatic number contain a triangle free graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$?
In [Er81] Erdős also asks the same question but with girth (i.e. the subgraph does not contain any cycle at all of length $\leq C$).

 For $r=3$, the question is exactly whether every graph $G$ of chromatic number $\mathfrak m$ contains a triangle-free subgraph of chromatic number $\mathfrak m$.
It may be worth cross-referencing Problem 1175 here. That problem records Shelah's consistency result giving a negative answer for $\kappa=\lambda=\aleph_1$: consistently, there is an $\aleph_1$-chromatic graph with no triangle-free subgraph of chromatic number $\aleph_1$. Thus, in that model, the present problem has a negative answer already for $r=3$ and $\mathfrak m=\aleph_1$.
So the statement for $r=3$ is positive for $\mathfrak m=\aleph_0$ by Rödl's theorem, as noted above, but it is not provable in ZFC for all infinite cardinals, assuming the consistency result quoted in Problem 1175.

A full proof 
claimed by Johan Land (using GPT-6-Astra, Fable 5.1, Gemini-3.8-Flash).
 Summary:
 I'm proposing a negative solution to Problem 740 in ZFC. The manuscript constructs a graph \(G\) with \(\chi(G)=\aleph_1\) such that every triangle-free subgraph of \(G\), not necessarily induced, is countably colorable. This would answer the question negatively already for the exclusion of triangles.
The construction is the comparability graph of the tree of injective countable ordinal sequences of positive integers with coinfinite range. This tree already appears in Bowler–Pitz. Uncountable chromatic number follows by diagonalization; the proposed key observation is a countable coloring of any triangle-free subgraph, where equal colors on an edge would force a triangle within that subgraph.
The host has \(2^{\aleph_0}\) vertices, so the claim concerns the unrestricted-vertex-set formulation. No CH assumption is used.

A partial proof 
claimed by GPT 5.6 Sol (using GPT 5.6 Sol).
 Summary:
 The proof solves the problem for $\mathfrak m=\aleph_0$.
Steiner recently proved that for every odd $g$ and every sufficiently large $k$, there exists $h_g(k)$ such that any graph with chromatic number at least $h_g(k)$ has a subgraph with chromatic number at least $k$ and no odd cycles of size less than $g$. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02522)
By the De Bruijn-Erdős theorem, for any graph with infinite chromatic number and any $N$, there exists a finite subgraph with chromatic number greater than $N$.
Construct the subgraph of $G$ as follows:
Pick an infinite sequence of positive integers $k_1<k_2<\cdots$. For each $k_i$, pick a finite subgraph $H_i$ with large chromatic number. This graph has a subgraph $G_i$ with chromatic number at least $k_i$ and no odd cycles of length less than or equal to $r$. Delete all vertices of $G_i$ from $G$, then continue for the next $k_{i+1}$. Finally, take the union of all of the $G_i$.
